title: Future Husband

jokes.text: Jack asking if he put a toaster waffle into his DVD player and watched it for an hour, then declared Nicole Kidman should get an Oscar for it
jokes.setup: Jack asks if he did something embarrassing while recovering from oral surgery under anesthesia
jokes.punchline: He put a toaster waffle in the DVD player, watched it for an hour, and gave Nicole Kidman an Oscar review for it
jokes.explanation: The absurdity escalates perfectly — it's not just that he was confused, it's that he had a fully-formed CRITICAL OPINION of the waffle's performance. The Nicole Kidman detail is perfectly specific and lands hard. Strong character integration: Jack's pomposity leaking through even his anesthesia stupor is very on-brand.

jokes.text: Liz reveals Jack was trying to order home massages off Craigslist, then a man appears at the door saying 'Hey, somebody order a massage?'
jokes.setup: Liz says it's a good thing she was there because Jack kept trying to order massages from Craigslist
jokes.punchline: A man immediately appears at the door — the order went through after all
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom timing executed with near-perfect economy. The setup is conversational, the punchline is immediate and physical. The follow-up — 'I already killed her!' — adds an extra layer of absurdist dark comedy that elevates it above a simple sight-gag payoff.

jokes.text: Liz shouts 'You're too late! I already killed her!'
jokes.setup: A man appears at the door claiming to be a masseuse
jokes.punchline: Liz panics and shouts that she already killed the client, playing into the dangerous-Craigslist-stranger joke
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy escalation — treating a Craigslist masseuse as a serial killer is funny, but Liz's instinct to immediately confess to murder is even funnier. Good economy and the follow-up 'Well played, Lemon' from Jack gives it an elegant button.

jokes.text: Jack on women jogging: 'Almost exclusively women that look like me. If the pervert community gets wind of morning jogging, God help us.'
jokes.setup: Jack is asked who else is out running at that hour
jokes.punchline: He describes the demographic as women who look like him, then ominously warns about perverts discovering jogging
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'the pervert community' is inspired — it treats perverts as an organized lobby group, which is vintage 30 Rock. Strong character integration as Jack speaks about himself with total unselfconsciousness.

jokes.text: Jack on CableTown: 'How could a company from Philadelphia buy a company from New York? That would be like Vietnam defeating the United States in a ground war.'
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses the idea of a Philadelphia company buying NBC
jokes.punchline: He uses Vietnam defeating the US as his analogy for an obvious impossibility — not realizing the US actually lost that war
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. Jack's blind spot is perfectly encapsulated: he uses an example of American invincibility that is factually the opposite — the US LOST the Vietnam ground war. The joke works on multiple levels: Jack's arrogance, his historical ignorance, and the irony that the very deal he's dismissing WILL come true. This is nearly at the 9.5 anchor level — exceptional character integration, perfectly earned, and it predicts the episode's entire arc.

jokes.text: Jack opens Don Geiss's book 'Geiss Cubes' to random pages and reads: 'Because a woman's brain has fewer folds' and 'The Negroid musculature...'
jokes.setup: Jack praises the 'timeless principles' in Don Geiss's autobiography and says he can open to any page
jokes.punchline: The random pages he opens to are overtly sexist and racist pseudo-science
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'timeless principles' to immediate racist and sexist content is executed with perfect comic timing. The 'Negroid musculature' line is so shockingly specific that it gets a big laugh while satirizing the era's corporate old-boy mentality Jack reveres. The truncation — Jack just putting the book down without comment — is economical genius.

jokes.text: Jonathan's excuse for Frank: 'On his way to work, he found some magic beans, and because he believed in them...' — then gets cut off with 'Ship up.'
jokes.setup: Frank called to say he overslept and asked Jonathan to make up an excuse
jokes.punchline: Jonathan begins an elaborate fairy-tale excuse about magic beans before being cut off
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jonathan is literally making up a fairy tale instead of a plausible excuse. 'Ship up' is a funny truncation of 'Shut up.' Good absurdist energy but the cutoff limits full payoff.

jokes.text: Liz finds 'Future Husband' in her contacts and has zero memory of how it got there
jokes.setup: Liz discovers someone labeled 'Future Husband' in her phone
jokes.punchline: She has no idea who it is, traceable only to being on anesthesia at the dentist
jokes.explanation: Solid premise establishment. Strong Liz-specific character comedy — her romantic life being determined by an anesthesia blackout perfectly reflects the character's hapless love life. Sets up the episode's A-plot economically.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I don't know what he looks like. He could be a serial killer. He could wear a thumb ring.'
jokes.setup: Liz is listing reasons not to call a mystery man
jokes.punchline: She escalates 'serial killer' with the equally-weighted dealbreaker of 'thumb ring'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The anti-climactic escalation from 'serial killer' to 'thumb ring' — treated with equal gravity — is perfect Liz Lemon character comedy. It's highly quotable, economical, and could only come from this character. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: Jenna's motto: 'Everything always works out for the best'
jokes.setup: Jenna tells Liz to be optimistic like her
jokes.punchline: Jenna's relentless optimism is immediately going to be undercut by the wallet-throwing demonstration
jokes.explanation: The line itself is setup for the wallet throw that follows. Mild laugh on its own but serves the episode's running gag infrastructure well.

jokes.text: Jenna throws her wallet out the window to demonstrate that 'everything always works out' — then looks confused when asked how that demonstrates anything
jokes.setup: Jenna says she's not worried about throwing her wallet away because everything works out for the best
jokes.punchline: Liz points out this doesn't prove anything; Jenna has no answer
jokes.explanation: Great visual absurdism — the non-sequitur logic of throwing away your wallet to prove cosmic optimism is perfectly Jenna. The pause after 'How was that supposed to make me call this guy?' sells it. Establishes a running gag that pays off later.

jokes.text: Tracy cannot remember the name of the network for a promo — 'Watch TGS this Friday on... on...'
jokes.setup: Tracy is filming an NBC promo for the show
jokes.punchline: He can't remember the name of the network he works for
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy Jordan moment — his cluelessness about his own workplace is a reliable character beat. The awkward silence of trailing off sells it. Competent but familiar territory.

jokes.text: Tracy declares himself 'a future Tony-nominated actor' mid-promo and announces he's going for the T in his EGOT
jokes.setup: After the failed promo, Tracy tells Liz she doesn't know who she's talking to
jokes.punchline: He reveals his Tony ambition, establishing the episode's B-plot, and announces he's going to 'keep it loose' for his one-man show — tonight
jokes.explanation: The EGOT gag is a series running joke and the 'keep it loose' response to 'have you prepared anything?' is a great Tracy Jordan character beat. His breezy confidence about an untested one-man show perfectly sets up the subplot.

jokes.text: 'Maybe we're the last people on earth. Maybe we are legend. You're Will Smith and I'm the dog.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Jonathan are alone in the building, Jack escalating his explanations for the silence
jokes.punchline: Jack jumps to an 'I Am Legend' apocalypse scenario and immediately casts himself and Jonathan in it — with Jonathan as the dog
jokes.explanation: The joke accelerates perfectly from 'last people on earth' to the I Am Legend reference to the devastating kicker that Jonathan is the dog. Jack has cast himself as the hero and his assistant as his loyal pet. It reveals the entire power dynamic of their relationship in one absurd riff. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jack fakes being in a meeting by saying 'Rhubarb, rhubarb, golf. Prostate.'
jokes.setup: Jack needs to pretend he's in a meeting to get off the phone with Avery
jokes.punchline: His simulation of executive meeting chatter is 'Rhubarb, rhubarb, golf. Prostate.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy. Four words that perfectly parody executive small talk: two nonsense filler words, two hyper-specific rich-old-man topics. The addition of 'Prostate' as a standalone utterance is the perfect button. Highly quotable, immediately funny, and only Jack Donaghy could deliver this with a straight face.

jokes.text: Jonathan says if anything should happen to him, he wants Jack to read 'Oh, the Places You'll Go' at his funeral; Jack flatly refuses.
jokes.setup: Jack sends Jonathan on a dangerous mission to the 'assistant underworld'
jokes.punchline: Jonathan's dramatic last request is for a Dr. Seuss book to be read at his funeral; Jack refuses without hesitation
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific joke — Jonathan's overwrought drama and Jack's ice-cold 'I'm not doing that' is a reliable dynamic. The choice of 'Oh, the Places You'll Go' (a graduation book) for a grown man's funeral is an inspired specific detail.

jokes.text: Dr. Kaplan has had a pamphlet printed up because he's 'tired of discussing' the cheese question
jokes.setup: Liz asks when she can start eating hard cheeses again after dental surgery
jokes.punchline: The dentist has pre-emptively printed a pamphlet specifically addressing this, because Liz asks so often
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon character work — her obsession with food is so consistent that her dentist has had to industrialize his response. The pamphlet detail is economical and specific. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: The dentist describes the mystery man's teeth: 'He has some gum recession. Four-pockets on 14 and 15. But overall, very good teeth. Especially for an Englishman.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks what the mystery man looks like
jokes.punchline: The dentist can only describe him in dental terms and concludes with the backhanded compliment about British teeth
jokes.explanation: Excellent professional-myopia joke — the dentist can only see people as their dental charts. 'Especially for an Englishman' is a well-worn but well-deployed stereotype that gets a laugh because of the clinical delivery. The dental terminology as a personality description is inspired.

jokes.text: Dr. Kaplan refuses to share more information citing 'doctor-patient confidentiality' — Liz says he's not really a doctor — and he responds: 'Then you're not really a patient. And people who aren't patients don't get toys from the treat bucket.'
jokes.setup: Liz challenges the dentist's status as 'really a doctor' to get him to break confidentiality
jokes.punchline: He retaliates by threatening to withhold toy access from the treat bucket — and Liz caves immediately
jokes.explanation: Exceptional scene. The escalation from professional dispute to toy-bucket negotiation is perfectly absurd. Liz's immediate vulnerability — 'But there's a Batman in there!' — is peak character work. The detail 'if you wind him up, he swims in the bath' adds an extra layer of specificity that makes it unforgettable. 'Damn you, Kaplan!' is a great button. High quotability.

jokes.text: Kenneth slept at the office because his keys are in Jenna's lost wallet; he reports that 'two little twin girls told me they wanted to play with me forever'
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains he slept at the office because his house keys are in Jenna's wallet
jokes.punchline: He describes creepy ghost children from The Shining appearing to him in the office at night, delivered with complete Kenneth innocence
jokes.explanation: A great dark horror-comedy moment that plays on Kenneth's character as possibly supernatural or cosmically disturbed. The Shining reference lands perfectly because Kenneth recounts it as totally normal. The ambiguity — is he traumatized? delighted? — is funny and a little unsettling. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Jenna slept in the office and was visited by 'two little twin girls who told me they wanted to play with me forever'
jokes.setup: Jenna explains she slept in the office
jokes.punchline: She describes a ghostly visitation (The Shining reference) as a casual, not-particularly-alarming overnight event
jokes.explanation: A Shining reference delivered with complete Jenna nonchalance — she's either genuinely unbothered by haunting or can't distinguish horror from hospitality. The casualness of the delivery is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Jenna sees a rave review about Tracy and dismisses the pun 'Claps-Giving Yay Harade' — 'It's as if Claps-Giving Yay Harade has lost all meaning'
jokes.setup: Kenneth shows Jenna a rave review for Tracy's show with the headline 'Claps-Giving Yay Harade'
jokes.punchline: Jenna is outraged by the cheap wordplay, lamenting that the phrase has 'lost all meaning'
jokes.explanation: Deeply meta — Jenna is offended by a meaningless pun headline the way people are offended by overused phrases. The pun itself ('Claps-Giving Yay Harade' for Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade) is intentionally terrible, which makes her passionate defense of its 'meaning' even funnier. Strong Jenna character work.

jokes.text: Tracy announces he's a Broadway star and asks Jenna to accept his Tony on his behalf — then says June is tough because he starts lifeguarding again
jokes.setup: Tracy announces he's a Broadway star after doing one show
jokes.punchline: He asks Jenna to collect his Tony at the June ceremony — then explains he can't attend because he lifeguards in June
jokes.explanation: The lifeguarding detail is excellent — Tracy Jordan has a secret wholesome side job that makes no sense for his character. The casual way he mentions it as a scheduling conflict is perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: Jenna explains she knows Tony rules because she's petitioning for a category: 'Living Theatrically in Normal Life'
jokes.setup: Jenna corrects Tracy about Tony eligibility rules
jokes.punchline: She only knows the rules because she's been campaigning for an entirely new category tailored to her own behavior
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jenna character joke — her narcissism is so total that she has lobbied an awards organization to invent a category specifically for existing as herself. 'Living Theatrically in Normal Life' is a perfect phrase that could only describe Jenna Maroney. High character integration.

jokes.text: Tracy demonstrates he 'never does the same thing twice' with rapid-fire random lines: 'Honey, I'm home! Pac-Man, I'm Jewish! Jeffrey, we lost the tournament!'
jokes.setup: Tracy claims he's a spontaneous actor who never does the same thing twice
jokes.punchline: He delivers three completely random, disconnected sitcom-style lines to prove his improvisational chaos
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Three lines that escalate in absurdity perfectly: a classic sitcom phrase, a non-sequitur identity confusion, and a completely unresolved plot reference. 'Pac-Man, I'm Jewish!' is a genuinely great piece of comic writing — nonsensical but oddly specific. Perfect Tracy Jordan energy. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jenna suggests Tracy find another T for his necklace — 'Do they give an award for Tarantula Misplacement?'
jokes.setup: Jenna tells Tracy if he won't do eight performances, he should find a different 'T' award for his EGOT necklace
jokes.punchline: She suggests 'Tarantula Misplacement' — a nonsense award that implies Tracy has lost a tarantula
jokes.explanation: Sharp absurdist gag that implies an entire unseen backstory (Tracy has lost a tarantula). Economy is strong — 'Tarantula Misplacement' lands as a complete joke in two words. Jenna's breezy delivery of nonsense is perfect.

jokes.text: Jonathan sings a little song to himself while downloading Geiss's schedule: '# Jonathan downloads Geiss' schedule / Mr. Donaghy will be grateful #'
jokes.setup: Jonathan is sent to find information about the secret board meeting
jokes.punchline: He narrates his own actions in a self-composed song, suggesting he's completely delusional about his own importance
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/audio gag establishing Jonathan's weirdness. Works as character comedy but is relatively thin — more of a transitional joke.

jokes.text: Liz has a 'donkey spell' — she makes donkey sounds in public — because she didn't fill her prescription
jokes.setup: Liz mentions she missed filling a prescription that keeps her from something, then immediately brays like a donkey
jokes.punchline: 'Don't worry, it's just a donkey spell' — treated as a known medical condition
jokes.explanation: A wonderful piece of medical absurdism — the 'donkey spell' is presented as a completely mundane known condition that just requires medication. The build (she says 'it keeps me from...' then immediately brays) is perfectly timed. 'Hee-haw, hee-haw!' as a recognizable condition name is inspired. Sets up a running gag that pays off twice more.

jokes.text: Liz's description of the mystery man: 'he is English and he made me laugh' — then Kenneth's enthusiastic response about England being 'the dried husk America came out of'
jokes.setup: Liz reveals what she learned about her mystery man — he's English
jokes.punchline: Kenneth calls England 'nothing more than the dried husk America came out of' with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Dried husk America came out of' is a memorable piece of writing — patriotic disdain delivered in Kenneth's cheerful, innocent voice makes it funnier. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Kenneth justifies deception for love using: 'Lot's daughters got him drunk to repopulate the world through incest' and 'Screech went to the masquerade ball in disguise so Lisa would kiss him'
jokes.setup: Kenneth says deceit is okay if done for love, and offers two examples
jokes.punchline: He pairs a horrifying Biblical incest story with a Saved by the Bell reference as morally equivalent romantic precedents
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The juxtaposition of Old Testament incest (Lot's daughters) with a Saved by the Bell subplot as equally valid romantic examples is a genuinely brilliant comic construction. Only Kenneth — sincere, Bible-quoting, pop-culture-obsessed — could deliver this. The specificity of 'Screech went to the masquerade ball in disguise' shows real craft. Approaches the top anchor.

jokes.text: Kenneth calls Wesley doing a fake Caribbean/Jamaican nurse accent that gradually goes Irish
jokes.setup: Liz and Kenneth devise a scheme to get Wesley back to the dentist's office so Liz can see him
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's fake 'Nurse Jamakaiah' accent starts Caribbean/Jamaican and drifts inexplicably Irish, culminating in 'Cool runnings, mon. Bobsled.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating failure of Kenneth's accent — 'You're going Irish!' — is a great bit. The payoff of 'Cool runnings, mon. Bobsled.' acknowledges the Caribbean-to-Irish drift with an absurd attempt to course-correct back to Caribbean. 'Bobsled' as a standalone closing non-sequitur is a perfect button.

jokes.text: 'Cool runnings, mon. Bobsled.'
jokes.setup: Liz is ending the call in her failing fake accent
jokes.punchline: She signs off with 'Cool runnings, mon' then just adds 'Bobsled' — apparently to drive the Jamaican point home or because she's panicking
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'Bobsled' as a standalone word — as if saying 'Bobsled' will authenticate her Jamaican accent — is perfectly stupid. The economy of just the one word makes it funnier than any elaboration would be.

jokes.text: 'Bobsled' — Kenneth says it as a standalone word after hanging up, apparently to reinforce the Jamaica theme
jokes.setup: Kenneth finishes his fake Jamaican accent phone call, having already said 'Cool runnings, mon. Bobsled.'
jokes.punchline: He says 'Bobsled' again after hanging up — apparently to no one, just to himself
jokes.explanation: A tight callback that reinforces the absurdity. Standing alone, 'Bobsled' after hanging up the phone — apparently to cement his own accent performance for himself — is economically perfect.

jokes.text: Liz has another donkey spell immediately after completing the call: 'Stay away, I will bite you! Hee-haw!'
jokes.setup: The donkey spell was introduced earlier as a condition manageable by medication
jokes.punchline: It recurs at an inopportune moment with the added detail that she threatens to bite people during the spell
jokes.explanation: The running gag escalates with the new detail of threatening to bite — which is funnier than the first occurrence because it adds aggression to the absurdity. A solid running gag callback.

jokes.text: Avery rejects Jack's romantic offer to braid her hair; he insists 'it's romantic and I'm really good at it'
jokes.setup: Avery says 'I told you last night, no' — Jack says 'Why would you even want to braid my hair?'
jokes.punchline: Jack defends hair-braiding as both romantic and a skill he takes pride in
jokes.explanation: Jack Donaghy's unexpected domesticity is a reliable source of character comedy. The straight-faced insistence that hair-braiding is both romantic and a genuine skill is a good absurdist-character moment. Gets paid off at the episode's end.

jokes.text: Jack barges into the CNBC newsroom shouting: 'Hey, CNBC! Nightly News rules! Go break a story, Williams! Nightly rules!'
jokes.setup: Jack enters the news floor looking for Avery
jokes.punchline: He announces himself by trash-talking CNBC on behalf of NBC Nightly News to Brian Williams specifically, like a sports rivalry
jokes.explanation: Jack's petty corporate loyalty extending to trash-talking competing divisions in their own building is good character comedy. The Brian Williams name-drop with 'Go break a story' is a fun media world joke.

jokes.text: Jack demonstrates how Geiss taught him to command a room: 'Back to work!'
jokes.setup: Jack says Don Geiss taught him to command a room with his voice
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates by bellowing 'Back to work!' — and it apparently works, though the moment is slightly anti-climactic by design
jokes.explanation: A mild character beat. The joke is that Jack demonstrates 'commanding a room' in the middle of a personal argument, which undercuts the drama. Competent but not memorable.

jokes.text: Avery says she cut ties with her old mentor 'Pat O'Brien, after he shaved his moustache'
jokes.setup: Avery tells Jack sometimes you have to cut ties from mentors
jokes.punchline: Her example: she cut ties from Pat O'Brien specifically because he shaved his moustache — a trivially cosmetic reason
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist character beat — framing moustache removal as a career-ending betrayal worthy of severing professional ties. The specificity of 'Pat O'Brien' grounds the joke in a very specific media-world milieu that's right for the show.

jokes.text: Jack defends his mentor loyalty: 'I have spent 30 years trying to be that guy.' Avery: 'But you're never going to be! Because no one is! That world doesn't exist anymore!' Jack: 'You're making me sound just like my mother!'
jokes.setup: Avery delivers a dramatic reality check to Jack about clinging to an outdated corporate ideal.
jokes.punchline: Jack's emotional response — 'You're making me sound just like my mother!' — implies the same speech is happening simultaneously somewhere in his family history, completely deflating the drama.
jokes.explanation: The punchline does double duty: it deflates the dramatic moment AND reveals that Jack has received this same intervention from his mother — suggesting a pattern of delusional loyalty. The phrase 'sound like my mother' applied to Avery's speech about a male mentor is a good misdirection.

jokes.text: Jack says he's going to Connecticut to 'stand by my man — which is the song I sang to Don at his promotion dinner'
jokes.setup: Jack declares his loyalty to Don Geiss and says he's going to Connecticut
jokes.punchline: He clarifies that 'Stand By Your Man' is literally a song he sang to Don Geiss at his promotion dinner
jokes.explanation: Great Jack Donaghy joke — his near-romantic devotion to male mentors has always been lightly homoerotic, and performing a Tammy Wynette song at a corporate dinner crystallizes that perfectly. The parenthetical clarification is the ideal delivery method.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'If I wanted to see a black guy make a fool of himself, I'd have sex with K-Fed again.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Jenna if she wants to support Tracy at his show
jokes.punchline: Jenna declines using a celebrity reference that also reveals she's slept with Kevin Federline
jokes.explanation: The joke works on Jenna's character level (her terrible taste in men, her casual racism) but relies on a 2010-era celebrity reference that dates it. The logic is also shaky — K-Fed is white. The joke may actually be a self-aware error about that, which adds a layer. Functional but not strong.

jokes.text: Jenna refuses to help Tracy — then when Kenneth says it would take 'the greatest acting coach the world has ever seen' — she immediately says 'Fine, I'll do it!'
jokes.setup: Jenna is firmly refusing to help Tracy with his show
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's flattery ('the greatest acting coach the world has ever seen') instantly breaks her resolve — she agrees immediately
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenna vanity joke — her ego overrides all other considerations the instant she hears a superlative compliment. Kenneth's timing in deploying it shows he understands how to manipulate her. Good structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Wesley arrives at the dentist's office and says 'Bobsled' to the receptionist after being told to sign in
jokes.setup: Wesley was told the appointment was urgent and the fake Jamaican nurse said 'Cool runnings, mon. Bobsled.'
jokes.punchline: Wesley walks in and simply says 'Bobsled' — apparently having internalized and accepted this as part of the appointment protocol
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Bobsled' is elevated by Wesley's earnest use of it as if it were a password or greeting. The one-word delivery, apparently sincerely offered to a confused receptionist, is a great payoff for the running gag. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Wesley reveals his phone shows Liz as 'Future Wife' — implying he also named her that while under anesthesia
jokes.setup: Liz was trying to secretly observe Wesley; instead he approaches her and asks about her phone label
jokes.punchline: He has her saved as 'Future Wife' — the exact mirror of her 'Future Husband' — confirming the anesthesia mutual attraction
jokes.explanation: A well-earned callback that pays off the A-plot setup symmetrically. The reveal that they both named each other the same way under anesthesia is a good romantic comedy beat that lands well in a show not normally focused on romance.

jokes.text: Wesley's story about why he was at the dentist: caused by an infection from 'off-brand toothbrush bristles' he bought 'over Christmas because my mom threw away my old Snoopy one'
jokes.setup: Wesley and Liz are getting coffee and he explains what brought him to the dentist
jokes.punchline: His dental crisis traces back to his mother throwing away his Snoopy toothbrush — he immediately acknowledges 'Wow, this is not interesting'
jokes.explanation: The self-aware 'Wow, this is not interesting' is the best part — he knows his story is terrible and says so immediately. The Snoopy toothbrush detail is charmingly pathetic for a grown man. Good setup for Wesley as an endearingly awkward character.

jokes.text: Liz mentions British people have notoriously bad teeth — Wesley claims he's never heard this
jokes.setup: Liz tries to make conversation by referencing the well-known British teeth stereotype
jokes.punchline: Wesley has genuinely never heard this — which is either deeply ironic or a running joke about British insularity
jokes.explanation: A well-worn stereotype that isn't elevated here. The scene is doing character work (they're awkward together) but the joke itself is familiar territory.

jokes.text: Wesley introduces the concept of 'breadback' — 'the loaf of back fat between a woman's bra and her giant underwear' — claiming it's a common phrase
jokes.setup: Wesley counters Liz's British teeth stereotype by offering an American stereotype — 'older women have breadback'
jokes.punchline: He defines 'breadback' with clinical detail, insisting it's a common phrase. Liz says 'people don't say that.' Wesley: 'Not to you, no.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and possibly the most quotable moment. 'Breadback' is a genuinely original invented term — 'the loaf of back fat between a woman's bra and her giant underwear' — presented as a common phrase that Liz simply hasn't heard. The button 'Not to you, no' is devastating and perfectly structured. The insult lands harder because it's delivered with total innocence. This competes with the top anchor jokes. High originality, perfect structure, and 'Not to you, no' is an all-time button line.

jokes.text: Wesley: 'Not to you, no.' (responding to Liz saying 'People don't say that')
jokes.setup: Liz denies that 'breadback' is a real thing people say
jokes.punchline: Wesley agrees — but specifies that people don't say it to her face, implying she herself has breadback
jokes.explanation: Three words that do enormous work. The implication is perfectly landed — Wesley is simultaneously insulting Liz, defending his invented concept, and being obliviously rude. Maximum economy. A near-perfect button on the breadback joke.

jokes.text: Jack Welch reveals Don Geiss has been dead for three weeks and they've been 'hiding him in the freezer — just like we did with Hiram Sheinhardt during the R.C.A. deal'
jokes.setup: Jack Welch reveals Don Geiss is dead; Jack asks if they've been hiding him
jokes.punchline: Yes — in the freezer, and this is apparently standard corporate procedure, as evidenced by having also frozen Hiram Sheinhardt
jokes.explanation: Extraordinary dark corporate comedy. The joke is that freezing dead board members to delay news until deals close is established GE corporate practice with precedent. The casual 'Just like we did with Hiram Sheinhardt during the RCA deal' is perfect — the precedent makes it institutional rather than ad hoc. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Welch reveals they hid Geiss in his freezer 'just like we did with Hiram Sheinhardt during the RCA deal'
jokes.setup: Welch explains they've been hiding Geiss's death for weeks
jokes.punchline: He reveals this is standard procedure — they have a historical precedent of freezing dead executives to facilitate corporate deals
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates the absurdity of hiding a dead man by normalizing it as corporate SOP. 'Just like we did with Hiram Sheinhardt' implies a long history of frozen executives, which is a deeply dark satire of corporate continuity at all costs.

jokes.text: Jack Welch offers 'weakness tissues' so Jack can 'pass some eye water'
jokes.setup: Jack Welch acknowledges Jack Donaghy may want to grieve Don Geiss's death
jokes.punchline: He offers 'weakness tissues' so Jack can 'pass some eye water' — refusing to use the words 'cry' or 'tears'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional vocabulary-based character joke. 'Weakness tissues' and 'eye water' are inspired euphemisms that perfectly capture the hyper-masculine corporate world's refusal to acknowledge emotion. The language itself does all the work. Jack's response — 'I'm not crying in front of Jack Welch' — is the ideal button. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jack refuses to cry in front of Jack Welch — specifically 'Neutron Jack'
jokes.setup: Jack Welch offers tissues; Jack refuses to show emotion
jokes.punchline: He won't cry in front of Jack Welch, clarifying the specific nickname 'Neutron Jack' as the reason — as if that makes all the difference
jokes.explanation: Good button on the weakness-tissues joke. The nickname 'Neutron Jack' adds a specific layer of macho corporate legend-worship that justifies Jack's emotional suppression.

jokes.text: Liz reports that the coffee date was so awkward 'the waitress gave us separate checks without asking. And a priest came over and asked us who we'd lost.'
jokes.setup: Liz reports that the date with Wesley was a disaster
jokes.punchline: The disaster was so palpable that a priest interpreted their vibe as grief — and the waitress preemptively separated their checks
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke that escalates beautifully. The separate checks establishes how bad it was, but 'a priest came over and asked us who we'd lost' is a genuinely original and hilarious escalation. The image of a priest ministering to the wrongly-grieving is perfect. One of the strongest jokes of the episode.

jokes.text: Jack delivers the devastating line: 'It's over, Lemon. It's all over.' — then reveals Don Geiss is dead and NBC is being sold to KableTown, 'with a K'
jokes.setup: Jack finds Liz after his Connecticut trip and delivers the news
jokes.punchline: The grand tragedy of NBC being sold is punctuated by the specific horror of the company being named 'KableTown — with a K'
jokes.explanation: The 'with a K' detail is perfect corporate horror — it's not just Philadelphia, it's a company that spells 'cable' with a K. Jack's devastation at this branding choice encapsulates his entire worldview. Also a meta joke for viewers who know this is NBC's real-life Comcast situation.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Oh, yeah, my parents have KableTown down in Pennsylvania. It's a fine and generous company.'
jokes.setup: Jack is devastated about NBC being sold to an unknown company from Philadelphia
jokes.punchline: Liz casually knows KableTown from her Pennsylvania upbringing and gives it a mild, working-class endorsement — the opposite of how Jack is treating it
jokes.explanation: Perfect class-gap joke. Liz's Midwest cable customer perspective on KableTown deflates Jack's corporate tragedy. 'Fine and generous company' as a TGS-level endorsement of Jack's worst nightmare is strong character contrast comedy.

jokes.text: In the middle of Jack's emotional breakdown about his career dreams, Liz asks: 'Will I still be able to turn in old cab receipts, or do you think—' then catches herself
jokes.setup: Jack is sharing his deep grief about his lifelong dream being destroyed
jokes.punchline: Liz's first concern is whether she can still expense old cab receipts — she immediately stops herself in embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Wonderful cringe comedy — Liz's mundane concern cutting through Jack's genuine emotional moment is perfectly calibrated. The 'I'm sorry' as she realizes what she's doing is great. Only Liz Lemon asks about expense receipts at this exact moment. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jack: 'That's the sound of me being erased from contact lists all around the world.'
jokes.setup: Jack is spiraling into self-pity about being the protégé of a dead man at a company that no longer exists
jokes.punchline: He claims he can hear the specific sound of mass-deletion from contact lists globally
jokes.explanation: A great piece of Jack Donaghy self-dramatization — his corporate paranoia is so precise that he can hear contact list deletions. The specificity ('all around the world') inflates it to proper Jack scale. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jack announces the Hug Plane is 'coming in for a landing' and gives Liz 'clearance for approach'
jokes.setup: Liz offers comfort; Jack says he heard something else
jokes.punchline: He announces an incoming hug using aviation metaphor — 'the Hug Plane coming in for a landing. You're cleared for approach.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most memorable moments. Jack using aviation control tower language to announce a hug is exquisitely in-character — he can't be vulnerable without a technical framework. 'You're cleared for approach' is an iconic line. High quotability, strong character integration. Rewatch-worthy.

jokes.text: Jenna's acting lesson begins: she says 'Acting is about consistency and control' — Tracy immediately says 'Got it, no farting'
jokes.setup: Jenna sets up a serious acting lesson
jokes.punchline: Tracy distills her abstract principle into a single concrete personal behavior note: no farting
jokes.explanation: Quick and economical. Tracy's interpretation of 'consistency and control' reveals his backstage behavior. The speed of the joke — no setup beyond the first sentence — is 30 Rock at its most efficient.

jokes.text: Jenna's elocution exercise: 'Repeat after me.' Tracy says: 'After me.' Jenna: 'No, Tracy.' Tracy: 'No, stop it, not this part.'
jokes.setup: Jenna begins an elocution lesson by saying 'Repeat after me'
jokes.punchline: Tracy literally repeats 'After me' — then 'No, Tracy' — perfectly mirroring every word without understanding the instruction
jokes.explanation: A classic verbal misunderstanding gag executed well. Not original (it's an old comedy bit) but Tracy's specific echo of 'No, stop it, not this part' extending the gag further than expected saves it. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jenna's elocution tongue-twister: 'To sit in solemn silence in a dull, dark dock...' — Tracy immediately destroys it: 'To sit in darkness in a sharp, shock shop in darkness in sitting in sharp.'
jokes.setup: Jenna performs a Gilbert and Sullivan tongue-twister perfectly as an elocution example
jokes.punchline: Tracy's attempt immediately collapses into word salad — 'in darkness in sitting in sharp' — followed by 'This is stupid'
jokes.explanation: Tracy's immediate disintegration of the tongue-twister into scrambled fragments is good physical/verbal comedy. The specific wrongness of 'in darkness in sitting in sharp' sounds like a man drowning in words, which is effective.

jokes.text: Jenna reveals her first acting job was as 'Baby Stuck in Well' in a commercial for 'Well Guards' — tagline: 'Guard your well... well.'
jokes.setup: Jenna defends the importance of acting craft — she's dedicated her life to it since her very first job
jokes.punchline: Her first role was 'Baby Stuck in Well' for a product called 'Well Guards' with the tagline 'Guard your well... well' — a useless and confusing product
jokes.explanation: Superb absurdist backstory joke. The product 'Well Guards' protecting against 'baby falling in well' is obscure enough to be hilarious, and the tagline 'Guard your well... well' — with its accidental homophone — is a great accidental wordplay that makes the company seem incompetent. Tracy's response 'You were a fat baby' is the perfect button. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Tracy responds to Jenna's childhood acting story: 'You were a fat baby.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has delivered an emotional speech about her dedication to the acting craft since childhood
jokes.punchline: Tracy's only response to this is a blunt observation about her baby weight
jokes.explanation: Economy is exceptional — four words that completely undercut Jenna's emotional moment. Tracy's total non-engagement with the speech in favor of a physical observation is peak character comedy. The bluntness is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Kenneth asks Tracy if he can repeat his performance — Tracy mishears it as an echo of his own voice
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks 'Do you think you can repeat your performance?'
jokes.punchline: Tracy echoes back 'Your performance' — as if he thought Kenneth was quoting him, or his mind simply mirrored the last two words
jokes.explanation: A quick Tracy-being-Tracy beat. Echoing the last words of sentences is a classic Tracy behavior, and it's funny here in context of him supposedly having learned about acting craft. Mild.

jokes.text: Wesley arrives at 30 Rock because Kenneth found his wallet — Liz reacts with utter disbelief: 'This is not possible.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth's lost wallet (from Jenna throwing hers out the window) has been found by Wesley — completing an absurd chain of coincidences
jokes.punchline: The universe has conspired to reunite Liz with Wesley through wallet logistics — Liz's stunned reaction: 'This is not possible'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed multi-episode callback that pays off Jenna's wallet-throwing, Kenneth's missing keys, and Liz's romantic plot simultaneously. The absurd logic chain is 30 Rock at its most structurally ambitious. 'This is not possible' from Liz is the appropriate reaction and sets up Kenneth's optimism callback.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'I am either very happy right now, or I'm having a pretty bad donkey spell. I'm okay. It will pass.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is overwhelmed by the miraculous coincidence of Liz's romantic fate being fulfilled
jokes.punchline: He's so overcome with emotion he might be having a donkey spell — then immediately reassures everyone he's fine
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the donkey spell gag. Kenneth using it as a measure of extreme emotional intensity — and then self-diagnosing and recovering — is perfect. 'I'm okay. It will pass.' as a stoic button is very funny. Strong character integration and the callback adds earned value.

jokes.text: Wesley and Liz agree to give it another shot — Liz asks if he likes Tex-Mex; he says no; she says 'See you there.'
jokes.setup: They've agreed to have dinner; Liz asks about Tex-Mex
jokes.punchline: He says he doesn't like it; she confirms the reservation there anyway — their mutual awkwardness is already the foundation of this relationship
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical character beat. Liz doesn't adjust when he says no — she just powers through. It perfectly captures both characters' social ineptitude and the show's overall tone about relationships. Great economy.

jokes.text: Avery's news report describes the frontrunner for running NBC as having 'the piercing, blue eyes of a Siberian husky that the job requires'
jokes.setup: Avery is reporting on Jack as the frontrunner for running the new KableTown acquisition
jokes.punchline: She lists his qualifications including 'piercing blue eyes of a Siberian husky' as a literal job requirement — delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke that works on multiple levels — it's satirizing cable news, Avery's personal feelings bleeding into her reporting, and Jack's specific vanity about his looks. 'Siberian husky' is a specific and weird enough choice to be genuinely funny. The deadpan news delivery makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Avery quotes Jack on-air: 'I'm going to celebrate by buying my lady friend that necklace she pointed out and then cooking her a Western omelette'
jokes.setup: Avery is reporting on Jack's role in the deal; she quotes him directly
jokes.punchline: His official quote to the press is not about the deal but about his personal domestic plans — necklace and omelette
jokes.explanation: Jack refusing to discuss the deal but going on record about his dinner plans is very on-brand — his personal life taking precedence over corporate matters when he's won. The 'Western omelette' as the specific celebration food is a great mundane detail that deflates the corporate triumph perfectly.

jokes.text: 'And then, I'm going to braid your hair.' — Jack says this on-air through Avery's news report
jokes.setup: Avery reads Jack's official quote about celebrating with a necklace and omelette
jokes.punchline: The quote continues with 'And then I'm going to braid your hair' — the hair-braiding running gag returns as Jack's third celebratory act
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff for the hair-braiding running gag. Jack putting his desire to braid Avery's hair into an official press quote — alongside the deal announcement — is absurd and in-character. The escalation of the quote (necklace → omelette → braid) is well-structured. Strong running-gag resolution.

jokes.text: Stock market report transitions into a credits roll of names being read alphabetically (apparently from a contact list being deleted)
jokes.setup: The news show continues; Jack said the sound he heard was contact lists being deleted
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts to names being read in alphabetical order over stock market graphics — implying we're watching Jack's contact list be deleted in real time, or it's the world grieving
jokes.explanation: An ambient joke that rewards careful viewers. The alphabetical name reading over market graphics is deadpan visual humor — but its connection to Jack's contact-list line requires attention to land. Clever structural joke.

jokes.text: Final audience reaction: 'Bravo! It's a triumph!'
jokes.setup: Tracy has spent five hours reading a phone book onstage
jokes.punchline: The audience responds with genuine rapture — 'Bravo! It's a triumph!' — confirming that random name-reading is apparently legitimate avant-garde theater
jokes.explanation: The payoff button on the episode's Tracy subplot. The undiluted rapture of the audience validates everything absurd about Tracy's approach to art and is a sharp satire of how critics and audiences respond to confidence over craft.

jokes.text: Tracy's second one-man show ends to thunderous applause: 'Bravo! It's a triumph!'
jokes.setup: Tracy has been through Jenna's acting lesson and is performing his second show to qualify for Tony eligibility
jokes.punchline: Despite everything we've seen — the failed elocution, the farting, the chaos — the audience apparently loves it; 'It's a triumph!'
jokes.explanation: A nice episode-closing beat that vindicates Tracy's chaotic talent. The juxtaposition of the disastrous rehearsal with the triumphant audience reaction is a satisfying structural payoff. The 'Bravo! It's a triumph!' is also callback to the rave review theme.

tmdb_overview: Liz searches for a man she met in her dentist's waiting room. Jack fears for the future when he learns a cable company may have its sights on NBC. Jenna helps Tracy try to get a Tony award.
insight: High-density absurdist hour delivers 70 jokes at 3 per minute, anchored by character-driven callbacks.
